summary: A proposal that the Network Information Center collect and keep answers to questions about what programs and services are available on the ARPANET, prompted by a MITRE request for information about resources of certain types. The idea became the Resource Notebook. It is a suggestion, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone suggested keeping one big binder where everyone can look up which computers have which useful programs, rather than asking around.

subtitle: A proposal to catalog what programs and resources are available on the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Researchers could not easily find out what programs and tools were available at different sites on the ARPANET.
tldr.mechanism: L. Peter Deutsch proposed that the Network Information Center (NIC) collect answers to resource inquiries and keep a searchable catalog.
tldr.outcome: The idea grew into the Resource Notebook, which served as an early registry of available services and tools on the network.

today: RFC 446 is a proposal that led to the Resource Notebook. It documents early thinking about resource discovery and network services.

sections.title: The Problem and the Proposal
sections.content: RFC 446 documents a proposal by L. Peter Deutsch of SRI. When researchers at MITRE asked for information about what kinds of programs and tools were available on the ARPANET (such as macro processors, data management systems, and wave analysis programs), it became clear that there was no central place to find this information. Deutsch proposed that the Network Information Center (NIC) become a repository for such answers, building a catalog that the entire network community could search.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone needed a special computer tool, no one knew where to find it. The proposal was to keep a central catalog.

sections.title: The NIC as a Repository
sections.content: The NIC already maintained a catalog and index system for the ARPANET Journal and computer-related documents. Deutsch argued that extending this system to include programs and documentation would not be a major undertaking, and it would bring immediate payoffs by making research sites more effective in discovering and sharing resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC already organized information, so adding a programs catalog seemed like a natural next step.

sections.title: The Broader Question
sections.content: Deutsch also raised a broader issue: what obligations does the ARPANET community have to serve as a resource to the outside world (particularly government agencies) versus its primary role as a research network? This tension between serving as a research platform and serving external information needs would shape network policy for years to come.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks whether the network should focus on helping researchers talk to each other or also serve other organizations.
